title: Neuro De-Armoring Cards, 7 November: section B's science

items.title: Excitotoxicity is calcium overload, not cells "vibrating to death"
items.where: B. The "Overheating" CPU: Glutamate Excitotoxicity, P3
items.comment: not so clear, you mean it is the over-excitement of the neurons or psychological over-excitement? if it's psychological over-excitement you'd need to explain how that's not a tautology and it also doesn't make sense like i can be overly joyful without being rageful so what excitement
items.my_version: The Mechanism: Excess Glutamate over-activates NMDA receptors, the doors on brain cells that glutamate unlocks, acting like a key stuck in the "On" position, so too much calcium pours into the cells. In extreme cases, like a stroke or a brain injury, that calcium overload kills them, which is what "excitotoxicity" means (Sattler & Tymianski, 2001). The anxiety, rage or "itchy brain" you feel in a glutamate storm is more likely the over-excitement itself than a sign your neurons are dying.
items.before: The Mechanism: Excess Glutamate over-activates NMDA receptors, acting like a key stuck in the "On" position. This causes "excitotoxicity"--literally vibrating cells to death. Subjectively, this feels like anxiety, rage, or an "itchy brain."

items.title: GluD: a new finding, still argued over, and the armor part said as a guess
items.where: B. The "Overheating" CPU: Glutamate Excitotoxicity, P4
items.comment:

if you are stating that something is a hypothesis then you have to explain how the hypothesis does or doesn't make sense, otherwise it's useless. and if apathy and schizotypy have never been tested, why are those in there, is there a reason other than gemini wrote something about them?
items.my_version: The Signal Dial (GluD Receptors): So if NMDA is the spark, is anything else turning the signal up or down? Well according to a recent finding by Johns Hopkins researchers, GluD receptors, mainly known for helping build synapses, are also channels themselves, gates that let current into the cell, and what opens them is D-serine (one of the tools below) and GABA, the brain's main calming chemical, rather than glutamate (Wang, et al, 2025). Other researchers' tests the year before found no sign of that, so it's still being argued over (Itoh, et al, 2024). A mutation that causes cerebellar ataxia, a movement and balance disorder, leaves the channel leaking when it should be shut, and in schizophrenia GluDs seem to be less active than normal (Johns Hopkins, 2025). Whether an armored state jams it too, on "High" as hyper-vigilance or on "Low" as apathy and schizotypy (odd, schizophrenia-like thinking), nobody has tested, so that part is a hypothesis.
items.before: The Signal Dial (GluD Receptors): Beyond the "voltage spike" of NMDA, Johns Hopkins researchers have recently discovered the brain uses GluD receptors as a master volume knob. While NMDA is the spark, GluD manages the baseline "hum" of the synapse. In an armored state, this dial is often jammed in the "High" position (Cerebellar Ataxia/Hyper-vigilance) or "Low" (Apathy/Schizotypy).

items.title: D-cycloserine is a different drug from D-serine, and its boost is small
items.where: B. The "Overheating" CPU: Glutamate Excitotoxicity, P5
items.my_version: D-serine may help therapy update old memories, because it switches on a spot on the NMDA receptor that this kind of learning needs (Wolosker, et al, 1999), and it may also open the GluD channels. The drug that's actually been tested with exposure therapy (facing the feared thing in small, safe doses) is a different one, D-cycloserine (DCS), which works on that same spot, and across 21 trials with over 1,000 patients it gave exposure therapy a small boost (Mataix-Cols, et al, 2017). It does not erase fear directly; it appears to strengthen whatever learning occurs during or after the exposure session. This is why session quality matters: if the exposure produces corrective learning and ends with reduced fear or mastery, DCS (and possibly D-serine also) may help consolidate that new memory; if the exposure is overwhelming or ends badly, it may consolidate the wrong association (Smits, et al, 2013).
items.before: D-serine may support therapeutic memory updating through NMDA-dependent learning mechanisms, while also engaging GluD receptors that regulate synaptic activity/tone. The specific drug form studied is D-cycloserine. which has evidence as an exposure-therapy augmenter because it can facilitate NMDA-dependent consolidation of extinction learning. It does not erase fear directly; it appears to strengthen whatever learning occurs during or after the exposure session. This is why session quality matters: if the exposure produces corrective learning and ends with reduced fear or mastery, DCS (and possibly D-serine also) may help consolidate that new memory; if the exposure is overwhelming or ends badly, it may consolidate the wrong association.

items.title: NAC works as a brake on glutamate release, not a vacuum
items.where: B. The "Overheating" CPU: Glutamate Excitotoxicity, P6
items.comment: why would you say it's a vacuum then say it's not a vacuum? arguing with yourself again here. make the whole guide coherent and useful.
items.my_version:
The Fix ("Lock, Stock, and Barrel"):The Vacuum (NAC): It works less like a vacuum than a brake. NAC gives the brain's support cells cystine (an amino acid), which they swap for glutamate, and in rat studies that glutamate outside the synapse trips a brake (the mGluR2/3 receptors) that cuts how much glutamate gets fired into the synapse (Moran, et al, 2005).

NAC: 1.8g – 2.4g (divided doses). Turns down glutamate release.
items.before:
The Fix ("Lock, Stock, and Barrel"):The Vacuum (NAC): Clears the flood by exchanging glutamate for cystine.

NAC: 1.8g – 2.4g (divided doses). Mops up glutamate.

items.title: Magnesium plugs the channel; zinc mostly makes it open less
items.where: B. The "Overheating" CPU: Glutamate Excitotoxicity, P7
items.my_version: The Lock (Zinc/Magnesium): Magnesium physically plugs the NMDA receptor's channel while the cell is at rest (Jalali-Yazdi, et al, 2018), and zinc mostly makes the channel open less often, with a weaker plug of its own (Amico-Ruvio, et al, 2011), so less of the voltage gets through.
items.before: The Lock (Zinc/Magnesium): Physically blocks the receptor channel to stop the voltage.

items.title: L-serine stays with a corrected reason; leucine goes
items.where: B. The "Overheating" CPU: Glutamate Excitotoxicity, P8
items.comment: chatgpt says the evidence is mixed, but forum evidence goes against the use of leucine, so cut it
items.my_version: The Repair (L-Serine): L-Serine is what the brain makes D-Serine from (Wolosker, et al, 1999), so it can feed the spot on the NMDA receptor (and maybe the GluD channels) that D-serine switches on, and help therapy sessions that end with low fear and a sense of mastery stick better. The conversion isn't very efficient though, so some people take D-serine itself instead (more risk, but also more benefit).
items.before: The Repair (Leucine/L-Serine): L-Serine is what the brain makes D-Serine from, so it can help recalibrate the GluD "Volume Dial" and make therapy sessions that end with low fear and a sense of mastery stick better. The conversion isn't very efficient though, so some people take D-serine itself instead (more risk, but also more benefit). And we use Leucine for structural repair, since it also tunes synaptic gain, which eases the "itchy brain" feeling.

items.title: D-serine turns things up, not down
items.my_version: Use D-Serine for acute sessions where you need to "force" memory reconsolidation. Best price from LifeLab. You should take it 45 minutes or so after taking PQQ & Ketones so that your brain is fueled when the D-serine starts working.
